text.en: The Mashgiach explains the Rebbe's extreme opposition not as harshness but as fear that a false geulah would take the place of the true one in people's minds.
He measures the Rebbe's battle against the Rambam's definition of Moshiach: only a king of the house of David who brings Israel back to Torah and the whole world to serve Hashem fits that picture.
The Mashgiach argues that the Rebbe's opposition protected even his opponents, who by their own admission planned with his reaction in mind.
He returns to his opening image: the sun is dim and the birds muffled now, until the day the sun shines bright with the announcement of Moshiach's coming.

The Mashgiach sees the very fact that bachurim come to a voluntary shiur, with no compulsion, tests or marks, as a present-day mofes fulfilling what tzaddikim said about the generation before Moshiach.
Heaven used the Zionist leader who wanted to save only Zionists, and who had refused the chassidim's money, to save the Satmar Rav, the great fighter against Zionism.

The Mashgiach reads Yosef's words to his brothers, that Hashem sent him ahead for sustenance, as the meaning of the Satmar Rav's rescue: Hashem saved him not simply so he would live, but so he would bring Yiddishkeit to America.

The loss of pre-war American Jewry was not because the grandparents were not ehrliche Jews; it was because the ehrliche rabbanim would not come to America, so there was no kashrus and no concept of chalav Yisrael.
The Mashgiach chooses the Stoliner story not because it was the greatest of the Rebbe's mofsim, but because it happened in public and everyone saw it.

The Mashgiach presents the revelation of the secrets of the Torah as three distinct stages: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed them, the Arizal spread them in preparation for Moshiach, and the Ba'al Shem Tov turned them into a way of serving Hashem.
The Mashgiach says that Rashi at times hints at secrets of the Torah in a comment; one who does not understand simply moves on, but one who understands sees the hint to the Zohar.
Before the Ba'al Shem Tov the Kabbalah of the Arizal was a 'dry' Kabbalah; the Ba'al Shem Tov showed how to use it while davening, learning, and even walking in the street and doing business.

Through the story of Gichon, the Mashgiach shows how close the redemption was in the Arizal's time: reopening what Chizkiyahu had stopped, against the will of the Chachamim, would have brought Moshiach, but the moment of favor passed.

Life itself, the difference between a living person and a body lying beside him, is something no scientist can explain; the Mashgiach identifies it with the soul, a spiritual force in the blood that one begins to grasp through the Torah.

The Mashgiach explains the prohibition of blood: an animal has a lower kind of life, and a Jew, who has a higher soul, should not take the animal's soul into himself; he may eat its flesh, but not its life.

The Mashgiach links the spread of Haskalah and Reform in Germany to the absence of Chassidus there: the lands the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim did not reach are where the decline, and later the destruction, began.
The Satan's threat to make his own chassidim is, according to the Mashgiach, visible where Chassidus has become rivalry, politics and team loyalty instead of serving Hashem.
The Mashgiach reads the separate gates, nusach and nesi'im of the shevatim, all bound to Yaakov Avinu, as the model for the many rebbes and groups among Jews: different roots, one whole.
Through the parable of grass that grows by the moon, a chassid may admit another rebbe is greater and still know he will grow only by the rebbe of his own root; by the 'sun' he would only burn.
Following the Haflaah, the Mashgiach treats the bond of talmid and rebbe like a shidduch: just as a bas kol announces a match before a child is formed, it announces which rebbe a talmid belongs to.
The Mashgiach says he may teach avodas Hashem beyond his own level because what he says is taken from sefarim and from what he saw by his rebbes, not his own.
A hardship whose purpose a tzaddik could not see at the time was revealed years later as the means of reaching another Jew.
Even a Jew who had married out long before was still in anguish over it, and the Rebbe in jail went over to him and tried to strengthen him.
At the engagement party, the drunken guests' insults against Jews were what made the father come to his senses.
Merely speaking about a tzaddik who has passed away arouses his merit to protect the Jews in a time of danger.
The Mashgiach draws the line from the story to the present: just as the Belzer Rav had people speak of an earlier tzaddik, today one should speak of the Belzer Rav himself.
Safety is not a matter of place: danger can reach anywhere, so in every place a person depends on Hashem's help.
The Mashgiach sees the spread of chadarim, Bais Yaakov schools and yeshivos across America today as the planting of one man.
Reb Shraga Feivel's insistence on being called 'Mister' is presented as an expression of his truthfulness, not merely his humility.
The Mashgiach sets the Gemara's warning against believing the world's praise against the Gemara's own rule that common opinion reflects reality.
Faith in the sages is presented as a parallel to faith in Hashem: the chachamim and tzaddikim of each generation are His messengers to lead the people.
The seven species are the praise of Eretz Yisrael precisely because they are the Torah's shiurim, and the shiurim are what bind a Jew to the chacham.
The vagueness of the measures is deliberate: a people that built precise structures in Egypt was given measures by hand and finger, so that it would need the rav constantly.
Frequent questions to the rav build a closeness through which the chacham comes to guide a person in kashrus, tznius and Shabbos as well.
The world's name 'tevel', read as confusion, describes hester panim: a night in which one sees only shadows until a flash of lightning shows everything for a moment.
'Shema Yisrael' is addressed not to Yaakov Avinu in heaven but to the bit of Yaakov's life within each Jew, who is a branch of his tree.
'Elokei avi' is measured concretely: if what was treif for one's great-grandfather is kosher for oneself, it is no longer the G-d of one's father.
Even a small change is a deviation, and the further the line runs the further it veers from the straight center.
Following the Chozeh of Lublin, the waters of Marah were bitter because the people were bitter; a talmid chacham is the 'etz' that sweetens them, since one takes 'etzah' from him with submission.
A Pesachdik dish is useless in a chometzdik vessel: the rebbe's word helps only one who makes himself a vessel to receive it.
A broken vessel is a whole vessel: the Karliner way of brokenness is what makes a person fit to receive.
The first stirring of redemption in Egypt was not wasted even when bondage grew worse; it was a seed, and the remembrance came after it.
A dream of a sin is not a real sin, yet it shows some connection to it; the Maggid's dream of a blessing in vain on Tisha B'Av planted a whole garden for the sitra achra.
Each book of Tehillim stripped another layer of the sitra achra's garden: fruit, leaves, branches, and finally the trunks.
When there is a decree, learning, davening or saying Tehillim creates a new heaven where the decree does not yet exist, and so it can be annulled.
On a cloudy Shabbos, one who says chiddushei Torah at the table makes a new heaven and feels the sun shine for him, even if his neighbor does not see it.
Even the learning and yiras Shamayim of those far from Chassidus comes from the holiness the Ba'al Shem Tov brought down into a sinking world.

The Mashgiach reads the Ba'al Shem Tov's wonders as lessons in emunah: for one to whom it is clear that Hashem makes the candle burn, it makes no difference whether it is wax or ice, a ship or a belt.

He compares the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim to the Avos: just as Yosef's and Sarah's tests put strength into every Jewish man and woman in Mitzrayim, the early chassidic generations put strength into the generations that came after them.
The Satan's task with Iyov, to break the barrel without spilling the wine, is the Mashgiach's picture of this generation's task: to stay pure in a place where it seems impossible.
Compared with earlier generations we are like small children who are given small tests, two times two instead of calculus, but our small tests are equal to the great tests of the earlier tzaddikim.
The word 'panim' is like an x-ray: the face shows what is inside a person, so different faces mean different inner natures, and each person is entitled to his own way of conduct.

Through the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach reads 'be warm at my hesped, for I will be standing there' to mean that the departed tzaddik puts the words into the speaker's mouth, so speaking about him is in a sense hearing him.

Every curse in Ki Savo can be turned to blessing by the Oral Torah, but the death of tzaddikim is not written at all; it exists only through the Oral Torah, so no further layer of Oral Torah can reverse it. The only remedy is that the tzaddik not truly be gone.

The difference between the bnei haneviim, who lost their prophecy when Eliyahu departed, and Elisha, who grew twice as great, is whether one carries on the tzaddik's Torah; the Mashgiach brings this from the Satmar Rav's own sefer.
Because every night of Chanukah was fresh for the Satmar Rav like the first, the Mashgiach sees meaning in his answering every night the Beis Yosef's question about the miracle of the first night.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's last words about clearing the vessels were a deliberate ruling that tzaddikim impart tumah, and he knew no error was involved because Chizkiyahu, the greatest master of tumah and taharah, came to greet him.
The Mashgiach presents the Satmar Rav, like Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, as the true 'doresh l'Tzion': precisely because he loved Zion he could tolerate no stain on its redemption.

Like Rav Ketina mocking the necromancer, the Kosel ruling was meant so that people not be drawn after the Zionists; its greater benefit was to the many who still go but, remembering it, are not drawn.

Amalek's war 'from generation to generation' means his tactics change with each generation; before Moshiach, like a losing army sensing the sword at its neck, he fights harder than ever to delay the end.

The Mashgiach reads 'vehayah eikev tishma'un', as the seforim of the Besht's talmidim do, as joy for Hashem in ikvesa d'Meshicha: the emunah of Jews in the heel of the exile is itself a great simcha above.
Just as the Megillah was unnecessary before Purim but indispensable after it, because a new era of hester panim began, so Chassidus is the new necessity of the era that began with the Besht.

The seforim of the Besht's talmidim are like the sample chapters an author releases before his book: a preview of the Torah that will be learned when Moshiach comes, the hidden Torah Rashi describes on 'yishakeini'.
Malachi, the prophet who speaks to the last generation, opens not with rebuke like Yeshayahu but with 'I have loved you', showing how the generation before Moshiach must be addressed.
Where Chassidus took hold, in Poland, Galicia and Russia, haskalah had no success until Chassidus weakened; where it did not, haskalah caused great destruction.

The Mashgiach reads the two titles of Moshe as two vantage points: Yehoshua could only write 'eved Hashem' because he could describe Moshe only from his own level, and so the Mashgiach, like a blade of grass that also benefits from the sun, describes Reb Shraga Feivel as an eved Hashem.

Shabbos is shleimus and shirah is harmony: just as a melody needs all seven notes, the seventh day completes creation, and a person who has all the parts in harmony has a neshamah of Shabbos and of song.
Eretz Yisrael, the seventh land, is a land of song, and the seventh sea, the Kinneret, carries the name of the kinor, the harp.
Since every leaf sings shirah to Hashem, tearing a leaf for no purpose interrupts its song, and a lone moving leaf among still ones is the chazan with the others answering.
The Mashgiach presents Reb Shraga Feivel's harmony between Hungarian Jews, Litvish roshei yeshiva and chassidus as an expression of his neshamah of shirah.
A niggun can outlast its singer: the Mashgiach says Reb Shraga Feivel's niggun is still sung in the yeshiva and in America, and his leaf will not be torn off.
The order of the generation mirrors the banners in the desert: each Jew draws through his officer of ten, fifty and a hundred, up to the tzaddik hador, whether or not people know who he is.

Pharaoh's complaint 'until when do you refuse to be humbled' means, with the Sfas Emes, that failing to be humble is one thing, but not even wanting to be humble cuts the last thread; a desire to have a desire still binds a Jew to Hashem.

The resentment of the wicked toward an ehrlicher Jew is envy, born of knowing deep down that he is better; that very pain is a hidden form of hachnaah, which is how they still draw from him 'from behind'.
Dovid was not punished for sins for which Shaul was, because Dovid's body came from a coarse root through Lot's daughter, and Heaven measures a person against what can be expected of him.
When a Hungarian Jew hates a Polish Jew, it is the bit of 'goy' each absorbed from his country's mazal that hates, not the Jew himself.

Later generations have more refined bodies, purified by generations of mesiras nefesh in galus, though earlier generations had greater souls; this is why sins recorded in Tanach seem incomprehensible to us.
The Mashgiach presents the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Ohr HaChaim as holding two parts of Moshiach's soul, the nefesh and the ruach, so that their meeting would have revealed Moshiach.
Because in the world of tikkun everything that lost its virtue regains it, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the day of the first luchos, carries a hidden power for the sprouting of the redemption.
Reading 'evyon' as one who longs for what he lacks turns the passuk about the poor into a description of Moshiach longing for Klal Yisrael.
The Mashgiach explains that Chazal's promise that one congregation's teshuvah would bring Moshiach has not yet come true because each generation is asked for a different level of teshuvah.
The 'hard heart' the passuk warns against is read as indifference to Moshiach's pain; a soft heart joins in his longing to come.

The Torah does not write 'and he died' of Hadar, the eighth king, while Ezra's pesukim do; the Mashgiach learns from this that each tzaddik records events by his own soul's root, which explains why Ezra placed Mordechai lower.
Haman's error was that he saw Moshe had died in Adar but did not know that Moshe was born in Adar, meaning that Moshe lives on in Mordechai, the Moshe of the generation.
Mordechai is mor dror, musk, which the Rambam holds kosher and the Raavad forbids; so too some judged Mordechai unfit, and mor dror equals in gematria 'on the seventh of Adar Moshe was born'.
Yaakov's dealings with Lavan's sheep, and all his work in Lavan's house, brought out deep Torah from hiding.
The first three names in the passuk form the initials of a shin, whose three heads allude to the three Avos, hinting that the men listed before Mordechai were counted by appearance alone.
On Purim the light of Mordechai's soul-root comes down, a light so great that even at Matan Torah no such light came down.
